key_points: Extended ACL entries match protocol, source address, destination address, and port, so they filter more precisely than standard ACLs.
Syntax order: access-list number action protocol source source-wildcard [operator port] destination destination-wildcard [operator port].
Wildcard masks are the inverse of subnet masks: a 0 bit means match, a 1 bit means ignore.
The operator eq matches one port, such as eq 23 for Telnet or eq 80 for HTTP.
Extended numbered ACLs use 100-199 and 2000-2699, and named ACLs use ip access-list extended NAME.
Every ACL ends with an implicit deny, so traffic not matched by a permit line is dropped.
guide.explanation: Outline week 7: Extended ACLs + Network Management covers writing extended ACLs that match protocol, source, destination, and port. Each entry specifies an action (permit or deny), a protocol, source and destination addresses with wildcard masks, and optionally a port operator. Entries are read top-down, and the first match decides the action.
guide.example: Block Telnet from 192.168.10.0/24 to any destination, and permit everything else. The wildcard for /24 is 0.0.0.255, so the lines are: access-list 110 deny tcp 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255 any eq 23, then access-list 110 permit ip any any. The first line matches TCP port 23 from that subnet, and the second line permits all other IP traffic.

questions.question: What is the wildcard mask for the subnet mask 255.255.255.192?
questions.explanation: Outline week 7: Extended ACLs + Network Management. The inverse of 255.255.255.192 is 0.0.0.63, because 255 minus 255 is 0 and 255 minus 192 is 63.

questions.question: Which port operator matches exactly one specified port in an extended ACL entry?
questions.explanation: Outline week 7: Extended ACLs + Network Management. The eq operator matches exactly one port, such as eq 80. The range operator needs two port numbers.

questions.question: Where should an extended ACL normally be placed?
questions.explanation: Outline week 7: Extended ACLs + Network Management. Extended ACLs are placed close to the source so that unwanted traffic is dropped before it crosses the network.

questions.question: Write the extended numbered ACL 110 lines that deny Telnet (TCP port 23) from 192.168.10.0/24 to any destination and permit all other IP traffic.
questions.answer: access-list 110 deny tcp 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255 any eq 23, then access-list 110 permit ip any any
questions.explanation: Outline week 7: Extended ACLs + Network Management. The /24 wildcard is 0.0.0.255, eq 23 matches Telnet, and the final permit line overrides the implicit deny for other traffic.

questions.question: What is the wildcard mask for the network 10.1.0.0/16?
questions.explanation: Outline week 7: Extended ACLs + Network Management. A /16 mask is 255.255.0.0, and its inverse is 0.0.255.255.

questions.question: Which access list number range is used for extended numbered IP ACLs?
questions.explanation: Outline week 7: Extended ACLs + Network Management. Extended numbered IP ACLs use 100-199 and 2000-2699, while standard numbered ACLs use 1-99.

questions.question: Why must an ACL include an explicit permit line when most traffic should be allowed?
questions.answer: Because every ACL ends with an implicit deny, so any traffic not matched by a permit line is dropped.
questions.explanation: Outline week 7: Extended ACLs + Network Management. Without a permit statement for the allowed traffic, the implicit deny at the end blocks it.

questions.question: Which command starts configuration of a named extended ACL called WEB-FILTER?
questions.explanation: Outline week 7: Extended ACLs + Network Management. The ip access-list extended NAME command creates or enters a named extended ACL. The ip access-group command applies an existing ACL to an interface.
